org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/ThingFactory.exploitability_evidence: The flagged sink is Class.forName(which) at line 40. Tracing backwards: 'which' is built at line 38 as "org.owasp.benchmark.helpers." + props.getProperty("thing"), and props is populated solely by props.load(thingproperties), where thingproperties is loaded at line 28 via ThingFactory.class.getClassLoader().getResourceAsStream("thing.properties") — a fixed, packaged classpath resource. The entry point createThing() is a static method that takes no parameters, so there is no attacker-controlled source (no request parameter, header, environment input, or external I/O) anywhere on the path to the sink. The value reaching Class.forName originates from a resource bundled inside the application itself; no sanitizer is needed because the source is trusted, and if thing.properties is absent or the class is invalid, the flow falls back to hardcoded Thing1/Thing2 in the catch/branch blocks. CWE-470 requires externally-controlled input to select the class; no such input exists here, so the flow cannot be completed by an attacker.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/ThingFactory.root_cause: The scanner flagged a Class.forName call fed by a configuration value, but the configuration value is read from 'thing.properties', a static resource packaged in the application classpath — not from any externally-controlled input. The method signature has no parameters, so no attacker data can reach the reflective instantiation. This is a helper class whose reflection target is fixed at build/deploy time by the application owner.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/ThingFactory.impact: None in this code path. Hypothetically, if an attacker could rewrite the bundled thing.properties (e.g., via a separate file-upload-to-classpath vulnerability), they could instantiate arbitrary classes in the org.owasp.benchmark.helpers package, but that would require a prior, unrelated compromise of the deployed artifact.
remediation: Keep the reflective lookup as-is or replace it with a whitelist map of allowed class names to eliminate the pattern entirely
If reflection is retained, validate props.getProperty("thing") against an explicit allowlist of permitted ThingInterface implementations

Ensure thing.properties and the deployment artifact are protected with integrity controls (signed JARs, restricted write permissions) so deployment-time files cannot be modified by the application runtime user

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: attacker-controlled Cookie 'BenchmarkTest00002' via request.getCookies() (line ~57), decoded with java.net.URLDecoder.decode(theCookie.getValue(), "UTF-8") into 'param'. Flow: fileName = org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.Utils.TESTFILES_DIR + param (line ~68) — direct string concatenation of the raw cookie value onto a fixed directory prefix. Sink: new java.io.FileOutputStream(fileName, false) (line ~73/flagged line 73) opens/creates the file at the attacker-influenced path; with append=false it also truncates existing files. Sanitizers on path: NONE for the filesystem sink — the only transformation, ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(fileName), is applied solely to the fileName echoed into response.getWriter().println(...) (HTML-output encoding for XSS), after the FileOutputStream has already been constructed, so it does not protect this sink. A cookie value such as '../../evil.jsp' (URL-decoded) traverses out of TESTFILES_DIR; exceptions in the try block are swallowed, so traversal attempts still execute the open. No validator, canonicalization (File.getCanonicalPath check), or FilenameUtils.getName() is applied anywhere on the path.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted cookie data is concatenated directly into a file path passed to FileOutputStream with no validation, canonicalization, or path-component stripping, allowing '../' sequences (or absolute-path injection depending on the filesystem) to escape TESTFILES_DIR.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Arbitrary file creation and truncation (empty content, since no bytes are written) at any location writable by the application process, enabling deletion/truncation of configuration or data files (integrity loss/DoS) and creation of files in sensitive directories; if the servlet later writes attacker-influenced content to the same handle or other code consumes the created file, this can escalate toward code execution.
remediation: Reject or strip path components: derive only a simple file name (e.g., org.apache.commons.io.FilenameUtils.getName(param)) and reject values containing '/', '\\', '..' or null bytes.
Canonicalize the final path (new File(dir, name).getCanonicalPath()) and verify it startsWith the canonical TESTFILES_DIR before opening, throwing/returning an error otherwise.
Prefer an allowlist of permitted file names or indirect identifiers (e.g., map a user-supplied key to a server-side filename) instead of concatenating raw input into paths.
Run the file-writing code with least-privilege filesystem permissions and log/HTTP-400 on traversal attempts rather than swallowing exceptions.

org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/Utils.java:1.exploitability_evidence: The flagged sink is Files.setPosixFilePermissions(script.toPath(), perms) in the static initializer of Utils.java (lines ~152-156). Tracing the inputs: (1) the target file comes from getFileFromClasspath("insecureCmd.sh", Utils.class.getClassLoader()) — the filename is a compile-time constant string, and the helper body shown only does classLoader.getResource(fileName), so no attacker-controlled source reaches the sink; the block runs once at class-load time on a file exploded out of the WAR. (2) The permission set is explicitly enumerated: OWNER_READ, OWNER_WRITE, OWNER_EXECUTE, GROUP_READ, GROUP_EXECUTE, OTHERS_READ, OTHERS_EXECUTE — GROUP_WRITE and OTHERS_WRITE are NOT added. The resulting mode is rwxr-xr-x (0755), which directly contradicts the finding's claim of 'read, write, and execute for all users'. Granting owner-write plus execute with read/execute for group/others is the standard, least-privilege mode for an executable script, and the code comment explains it is a workaround to restore the execute bit lost when the script is exploded from the WAR. There is no world-writable file, no attacker influence over path or permissions, and this is OWASP Benchmark test-harness scaffolding (org/owasp/benchmark/helpers), not application security logic. The rule misfired on a safe API usage.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/Utils.java:1.root_cause: Scanner over-report: the rule assumes a set containing read+write+execute is 'permissive for all users', but the actual set (0755) grants write only to the owner, which is the conventional mode for an executable script. The filename is a hardcoded constant and the operation is a deliberate, commented workaround in benchmark helper code.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/Utils.java:1.impact: None. Even hypothetically, the affected file is a benchmark test script (insecureCmd.sh) inside the application's own deployment, and the applied 0755 mode matches standard executable permissions, so there is no privilege-escalation or information-leakage path attributable to this code.
remediation: No code change required; suppress this finding for the benchmark helper or add a path/note exclusion for org/owasp/benchmark/helpers.
Optionally tighten the Semgrep rule to only fire when OTHERS_WRITE or GROUP_WRITE is added, so 0755-style executable permissions are not flagged.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: HTTP cookie value read at lines 56-66 — the cookie named 'BenchmarkTest00001' is taken from request.getCookies() and passed through java.net.URLDecoder.decode(theCookie.getValue(), "UTF-8"), which only decodes percent-encoding and performs no path sanitization ('../' and encoded '%2e%2e%2f' survive). The value flows into `param`, then line 71: `fileName = org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.Utils.TESTFILES_DIR + param;` — a plain string concatenation onto a constant directory prefix with no canonicalization or containment check. The flagged sink at line 72 is `new java.io.FileInputStream(new java.io.File(fileName))`, which opens whatever file the concatenated path resolves to. The only sanitization visible on the path, ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(...), is applied AFTER the file read, only to the string echoed into the HTTP response — it is an HTML output encoder for the XSS sink and is not applied to (nor adequate for) the file-path sink. A request with cookie BenchmarkTest00001=../../../../etc/passwd (URL-encoded) therefore makes the servlet open and return the contents of an arbitrary file.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: User-controlled cookie data is concatenated directly into a file path and opened for reading without canonicalization or validation that the resolved path remains within the TESTFILES_DIR base directory; the only encoding present (ESAPI encodeForHTML) targets the response writer, not the file API.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Arbitrary file read on the server: an attacker can traverse outside the intended directory (e.g. '../../../etc/passwd', application config, property files with credentials) and have the file's first 1000 bytes echoed back in the HTTP response, enabling disclosure of sensitive data and potentially facilitating further attacks.
remediation: Canonicalize the resolved path (new File(TESTFILES_DIR, param).getCanonicalPath()) and reject the request unless it starts with the canonical TESTFILES_DIR prefix
Or reduce input to a bare filename with org.apache.commons.io.FilenameUtils.getName(param) and reject values containing '/', '\\', or null bytes
Prefer an indirect allowlist: map user-supplied identifiers to server-side file names instead of building paths from raw input

org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/DatabaseHelp.exploitability_evidence: The flagged sink is `stmt.executeUpdate(sql)` at line 174 inside `private static void executeSQLCommand(String sql)`. On the visible path, the value flows directly from the method parameter `sql` into the raw `Statement.executeUpdate` call with no sanitization, validation, allow-listing, or parameterization; the called helper `getSqlStatement()` (body shown) only lazily creates a plain `java.sql.Statement` from the `BenchmarkDB` DataSource connection (`conn.createStatement()`) and performs no cleansing, so there is no sanitizer on the path from parameter to sink. However, `executeSQLCommand` is private and none of its callers or any attacker-controlled source (e.g., an HTTP request parameter reaching `sql`) are shown in the provided code, so attacker control of the string cannot be established from what is visible.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/DatabaseHelp.root_cause: The method is a real, unsanitized SQL execution sink: it runs an arbitrary string through `Statement.executeUpdate` instead of a parameterized `PreparedStatement`. The internal path (parameter -> sink) contains no encoding or validation, but the code shown does not reveal whether any caller passes attacker-controlled data or only trusted/constant SQL strings, and exploitability therefore cannot be proven or refuted from the evidence provided.
org/owasp/benchmark/helpers/DatabaseHelp.impact: If any caller passes user-controllable input into this helper, an attacker could execute arbitrary SQL against the BenchmarkDB (data exfiltration, modification, or deletion), i.e., classic CWE-89 SQL injection.
remediation: Refactor helpers to use `connection.prepareStatement(...)` with `?` placeholders and bind values via `setString`/`setInt` instead of concatenating or formatting SQL strings.

The decoded value is concatenated directly into the query: 'String sql = "INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('foo','" + param + "')"'. The sink at line 59 is 'statement.executeUpdate(sql)', where 'statement' comes from DatabaseHelper.getSqlStatement(), whose body (shown) calls 'conn.createStatement()' — a plain java.sql.Statement, not a PreparedStatement, so the query string is parsed as-is with no parameterization. No escaping, validation, or sanitization adequate for the SQL-execution sink exists anywhere on the path (the ESAPI encodeForHTML in outputUpdateComplete only affects the echoed response, not the executed SQL). A payload like foo','bar')-- in the header breaks out of the string literal and is executed.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Unsanitized attacker-controlled HTTP header value is string-concatenated into a SQL INSERT statement and executed via a non-parameterized java.sql.Statement (Statement.executeUpdate), allowing injection into the SQL grammar.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: An attacker can modify the executed SQL (e.g., terminate the value literal and inject additional statements/clauses), enabling tampering with or exfiltration of database contents, insertion of arbitrary rows, and potentially broader database compromise depending on the DB user's privileges.
remediation: Replace Statement with a PreparedStatement: use 'connection.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('foo', ?)")' and bind the header-derived value via setString(1, param).
Do not build SQL by string concatenation with any request-derived input (headers, parameters, cookies).
As defense in depth, validate/normalize the input against an allowlist where feasible, and ensure the DB account used has least-privilege permissions.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: request.getHeaders("BenchmarkTest00018") — the first header value is taken (line 46-48, param = headers.nextElement()). The value is URL-decoded with java.net.URLDecoder.decode(param, "UTF-8") (line 52), which is NOT a SQL sanitizer (it merely decodes percent-escapes and can even restore quote characters). The decoded value is then concatenated directly into SQL: "INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('foo','" + param + "')" (line 54). Sink: DatabaseHelper.getSqlStatement() (body shown) returns a plain java.sql.Statement via conn.createStatement() — no PreparedStatement/parameter binding — and statement.executeUpdate(sql) executes the attacker-tainted string (lines 57-59). No sanitizer, validator, or encoder adequate for the SQL sink exists anywhere on this path; the ESAPI encodeForHTML in outputUpdateComplete only HTML-escapes the echoed SQL after execution and is irrelevant to SQL injection. An attacker can send header 'BenchmarkTest00018: x'),('bar' -- to inject arbitrary SQL.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Unsanitized HTTP header value is concatenated into a dynamically-built SQL INSERT statement and executed via a non-parameterized java.sql.Statement, allowing attacker-controlled SQL syntax (CWE-89).
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Full SQL injection against the BenchmarkDB datasource: an attacker can modify query semantics, insert/alter or exfiltrate data, and depending on DB privileges execute stacked statements or destructive operations; note also that SQL exceptions may be rethrown and leak details if hideSQLErrors is false.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a java.sql.PreparedStatement using a placeholder: INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES (?, ?) and bind param via statement.setString(2, param)
Never build SQL from request-derived values; enforce parameterized queries via code review and SAST gates
As defense-in-depth, validate/normalize the header input to the expected format (e.g., username charset allowlist) and ensure database accounts use least privilege

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: `request.getHeaders("BenchmarkTest00017")` in BenchmarkTest00017.java — the first header element is fully attacker-controlled (an HTTP request header set by the client). The value is assigned to `param`, then passed through `java.net.URLDecoder.decode(param, "UTF-8")`, which only percent-decodes and does not neutralize command metacharacters (it actually turns an encoded `%26` into a live `&`). On Windows, `Utils.getOSCommandString("echo")` (body shown) returns the prefix `"cmd.exe /c echo "`. At line 63 the flagged sink executes `r.exec(cmd + param)` — raw concatenation of the tainted header value into the command string with no whitelist, validation, escaping, or shell-safe quoting anywhere on the path. The only sanitizer present is ESAPI `encodeForHTML`, applied in `Utils.printOSCommandResults` to the command OUTPUT before writing to the response; it mitigates reflected XSS in the results but has zero effect on the exec() sink. On Windows the command runs under `cmd.exe /c`, which interprets metacharacters, so a header value like `a& whoami` yields `cmd.exe /c echo a& whoami`, executing an attacker-chosen command; on non-Windows, Runtime.exec(String) tokenizes without a shell, weakening but not removing the sink concern. Complete source-to-sink trace with no adequate sanitizer for this sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: An untrusted HTTP header value is URL-decoded and concatenated directly into a string passed to Runtime.exec(), with the Windows branch explicitly invoking `cmd.exe /c`, allowing arbitrary shell metacharacters from the client to alter or chain OS commands. No input validation, allowlisting, or command-safe API (e.g., argument-array exec) is used.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Remote, unauthenticated OS command injection: an attacker controlling the 'BenchmarkTest00017' request header can execute arbitrary operating-system commands on the host (on Windows via cmd.exe metacharacters such as `&`, `|`, `&&`), enabling code execution, data theft, lateral movement, or full server compromise.
remediation: Do not pass user-supplied input into OS command strings; replace the echo/OS-command use case with a Java-native equivalent (e.g., log the value or return it) whenever possible.
If OS commands are unavoidable, validate the input against a strict server-side allowlist of known-good values (e.g., an enumerated set) before use; reject anything else.

Never concatenate raw input into a single command string; use Runtime.exec(String[])/ProcessBuilder with the command and each argument as separate elements, and avoid `cmd.exe /c` shells so metacharacters are not interpreted.
As defense in depth, keep the ESAPI output encoding already present, but recognize it does not mitigate command injection — input handling at the exec sink is the required fix.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: request.getParameter("BenchmarkTest00025") at line 44 returns fully attacker-controlled HTTP input (defaulting to "" only when null). The value flows with no transformation into the string concatenation at line 48: sql = "SELECT userid from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + param + "'", then into the flagged sink at lines 51-53: DatabaseHelper.JDBCtemplate.queryForObject(sql, Long.class), which executes the attacker-appended string as SQL. No sanitizer exists on this path: the null check is not sanitization, and org.owasp.esapi.ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(sql) is applied only in the EmptyResultDataAccessException catch block to HTML-encode the query for HTTP output — it runs after (or instead of) query execution and is an HTML encoder, not a SQL encoder, so it cannot neutralize the SQL sink. A payload such as BenchmarkTest00025=x' OR '1'='1 directly alters query semantics.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted HTTP request parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL query string instead of being bound via a parameterized statement; the only encoder present (ESAPI encodeForHTML) targets the HTML output sink in the exception path, not the SQL execution sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: An unauthenticated attacker can manipulate the executed SQL to extract or modify database contents (e.g., dump the USERS table), and depending on DBMS configuration potentially achieve blind injection, data tampering, or further compromise.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized query: org.springframework.jdbc.core.JdbcTemplate.queryForObject("SELECT userid from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='?'", Long.class, param)
If dynamic SQL is ever required, apply strict server-side allowlist validation and DB-side least privilege; remove reliance on output encoding (encodeForHTML), which does not address SQL injection

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: `request.getParameter("BenchmarkTest00024")` (HTTP parameter, line 44), with only a null-check default to "" and no sanitization/encoding applied. The value is concatenated directly into the SQL text at line 49: `String sql = "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME=? and PASSWORD='" + param + "'"`. The tainted string is then passed to `connection.prepareStatement(sql, ...)` (lines 52-55) and executed via `statement.execute()` (line 57). Although PreparedStatement is used, it provides no protection here: the placeholder only covers USERNAME, which is bound to the constant "foo" via `statement.setString(1, "foo")`, while the attacker-controlled `param` is embedded in the SQL text BEFORE compilation. A value such as `x' OR '1'='1` (or a UNION SELECT payload) closes the quote and injects SQL. The ESAPI encoding in DatabaseHelper.printResults applies only to HTTP output (XSS mitigation), not to the SQL sink, so it does not neutralize this injection. This is the classic insecure PreparedStatement pattern the OWASP Benchmark encodes as vulnerable.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted HTTP request data is string-concatenated into the SQL statement text instead of being bound as a parameter; the PreparedStatement placeholder covers only one of two user values, and the tainted value is baked into the statement before prepareStatement() is called.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: An attacker can manipulate the SQL query to bypass authentication-style filters (e.g., OR '1'='1), extract additional data via UNION-based injection, and, depending on the JDBC driver/database configuration, potentially execute stacked statements — leading to disclosure or manipulation of the USERS table and other database content.
remediation: Parameterize the user value too: use `SELECT * FROM USERS WHERE USERNAME=? AND PASSWORD=?` and call statement.setString(2, param) (and ideally statement.setString(1, username)) so no untrusted data is concatenated into SQL.
Never build SQL by string concatenation of request data; enforce this via code review and SAST gating.
As defense-in-depth, validate/allowlist expected input formats (e.g., username charset, password length) and grant the application DB account least-privilege access.
Keep `DatabaseHelper.hideSQLErrors` semantics safe: avoid leaking raw SQLException details to clients when it is false.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: `request.getParameter("BenchmarkTest00026")` (attacker-controlled HTTP request parameter, defaulting to "" if null). The raw value is concatenated directly into the SQL string at line 49: `String sql = "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + param + "'"`. The tainted `sql` is then passed as the sole argument to the sink `org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.DatabaseHelper.JDBCtemplate.queryForRowSet(sql)` (lines 50-51), which executes it as a dynamic statement. No sanitizer, validator, or encoder is applied to `param` between source and sink. The ESAPI `encodeForHTML` calls present in the method are output encoding applied AFTER query execution (to query results and to the `sql` echoed in the EmptyResultDataAccessException handler); they mitigate reflected XSS in the response but do nothing to neutralize SQL metacharacters in the query itself. The query is not parameterized. A payload like `?BenchmarkTest00026=' OR '1'='1` or `';--` breaks out of the PASSWORD literal and alters query semantics, confirming an exploitable SQL injection.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted HTTP request parameter is concatenated into a SQL statement string and executed via JdbcTemplate.queryForRowSet without parameterization or input validation; the only encoding present (ESAPI encodeForHTML) is applied to output, not to the SQL input.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Full SQL injection: an attacker can manipulate query logic to bypass authentication-style conditions, dump or modify database contents (e.g., USERS table), and depending on database/driver capabilities achieve data exfiltration via error- or time-based techniques or stacked queries.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized query: `JDBCtemplate.queryForRowSet("SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD=?", param)`, letting the JDBC driver bind the value safely.
As defense in depth, validate/whitelist the expected input format for the parameter before use, and ensure database accounts used by the application follow least privilege.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: request.getParameter("BenchmarkTest00027") (line 44) — raw HTTP input with no validation, only a null-to-empty-string default. The value is concatenated directly into SQL at line 48: String sql = "INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('foo','" + param + "')";. The tainted string is passed to statement.executeUpdate(sql) (line 52), where statement is produced by DatabaseHelper.getSqlStatement(), whose body (shown) calls conn.createStatement() — a plain java.sql.Statement, not a PreparedStatement, so no parameterization exists. No sanitizer, validator, or encoder touches param anywhere on this path. The ESAPI encodeForHTML call in DatabaseHelper.outputUpdateComplete operates on the SQL string only after execution and only for HTML output rendering; it does not neutralize SQL metacharacters at the executeUpdate sink. A payload such as BenchmarkTest00027=xyz');-- or a value containing a single quote breaks out of the quoted value and alters the INSERT statement, proving exploitability.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted HTTP request parameter is concatenated into a dynamically built SQL string that is executed via a non-parameterized java.sql.Statement; there is no escaping, allowlisting, or use of PreparedStatement placeholders on the path.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: An attacker can alter the structure of the INSERT statement, inject arbitrary values into the users table (e.g., planting credentials), attempt stacked queries or database-specific syntax abuse depending on the driver/JDBC URL, and potentially exfiltrate or corrupt data. SQL exceptions may also leak schema details if DatabaseHelper.hideSQLErrors is false.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a java.sql.PreparedStatement using a placeholder: INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('foo', ?), and bind param via setString(1, param).
Add server-side input validation/allowlisting on the parameter before use as defense in depth.
Ensure DatabaseHelper.getSqlStatement pattern is not reused for tainted SQL; add a code-review/CI rule forbidding concatenation of request data into SQL strings.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: HTTP request parameter `request.getParameter("BenchmarkTest00027")` (line 45). The value flows unmodified into `param`, then is concatenated directly into the SQL string at line 49: `String sql = "INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('foo','" + param + "')"`. The string is then passed to `statement.executeUpdate(sql)` at line 52 — the flagged sink — where `statement` is a plain `java.sql.Statement` created via `DatabaseHelper.getSqlStatement()` (confirmed from the shown helper body: `conn.createStatement()`, no PreparedStatement, no parameterization). No sanitizer, validator, or encoder is applied to `param` anywhere on this path. The only encoding in the flow is `ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(sql)` inside `DatabaseHelper.outputUpdateComplete`, but it executes AFTER `executeUpdate` and only HTML-encodes the query for output to the HTTP response — it does not neutralize SQL metacharacters for the SQL-execution sink. A payload like `foo'); DROP TABLE users;--` or `x','y'); --` injected via the parameter reaches the database engine as SQL.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted HTTP parameter is concatenated into a SQL INSERT statement and executed via java.sql.Statement.executeUpdate instead of a parameterized PreparedStatement, allowing an attacker to break out of the single-quoted string literal and inject arbitrary SQL.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Full SQL injection: an attacker can modify query structure to exfiltrate or tamper with database contents, create/modify/delete rows or tables, and depending on database privileges and configuration execute OS commands, read files, or escalate to remote code execution.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a PreparedStatement using a bind parameter: `PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('foo', ?)"); ps.setString(1, param);`
Apply strict input validation on the parameter (e.g., allow-list of permitted characters/length) as defense in depth, but do not rely on it as the primary control.
Avoid exposing raw SQL or the query string back to the user in responses (as outputUpdateComplete does) to prevent information leakage.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: HTTP request parameter read at lines ~43-48 — `request.getParameterMap()`, then `param = values[0]` for parameter name "BenchmarkTest00028"; this value is fully attacker-controlled. Taint flow: `param` flows unchanged into `fileName = org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.Utils.TESTFILES_DIR + param;` (line ~57) — a plain string concatenation with a constant directory prefix, so any `../` sequence in the parameter escapes the TESTFILES_DIR base. Sink: `new java.io.FileOutputStream(fileName, false)` (line ~70), which opens/creates (and with append=false truncates) the file at the attacker-chosen path. Sanitization check: the only transform on the path, `org.owasp.esapi.ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(fileName)`, is applied solely to the value echoed to the response writer, NOT to the value passed to the FileOutputStream, and is an HTML-output encoder anyway — it neither canonicalizes nor restricts path components. There is no FilenameUtils.getName(), no normalize/startsWith containment check, and no validation of `param` anywhere on the source-to-sink path. Example exploit: GET/POST with BenchmarkTest00028=../../../../etc/owasp_test or ..\..\..\Windows\Temp\x.tmp creates/truncates files outside TESTFILES_DIR subject to process permissions.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Unvalidated, attacker-controlled HTTP parameter is concatenated directly onto a directory constant and used as the pathname for a FileOutputStream. The path is never canonicalized, stripped of directory-traversal components, or confined to the intended TESTFILES_DIR, so '../' sequences in the parameter escape the base directory. The ESAPI encodeForHTML call present in the method only protects the response echo and does not sanitize the file-open path.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Arbitrary file creation and truncation (append=false) at any location writable by the application's process user. While the file content is not attacker-controlled (nothing is written before close), an attacker can overwrite/truncate existing files (configuration, logs, lock files) causing denial of service or state corruption, plant empty files in sensitive directories to disrupt other components, or create files as a foothold for chained exploits.
remediation: Reject or strip directory components from user input before use in file paths, e.g. `fileName = Utils.TESTFILES_DIR + org.apache.commons.io.FilenameUtils.getName(param);`
Canonicalize and enforce containment: resolve with java.nio.file.Paths.get(TESTFILES_DIR, param).normalize() and verify result.startsWith(Paths.get(TESTFILES_DIR)) before opening; reject otherwise.
Prefer indirection: map user-supplied identifiers to server-side filenames via an allowlist (or database key) rather than building paths from raw input.
Run the application with least-privilege filesystem permissions so even a residual traversal cannot reach sensitive paths.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: attacker-controlled HTTP parameter `request.getParameter("BenchmarkTest00021")` (only null-checked, not sanitized). Flow: `param` is concatenated raw into the filter string at line 56: `String filter = "(&(objectclass=person))(|(uid=" + param + ")(street={0}))";`. The flagged sink is `ctx.search(base, filter, filters, sc)` at line 58, where `filter` is passed directly as the search filter to the JNDI DirContext (obtained via LDAPManager.getDirContext -> InitialDirContext(createEnv()), which binds to ldap://localhost:10389 as admin with no restriction relevant to taint). The Object[] `filters` only fills the {0} placeholder with the constant "The streetz 4 Ms bar"; the attacker value `param` bypasses this safe parameterization mechanism entirely via string concatenation. No sanitizer exists on the path: the only encoder calls (ESAPI encodeForHTML) are applied AFTER the search, to the LDAP results and the filter echoed in the 'nothing found' branch — HTML output encoding is not adequate for an LDAP filter sink (CWE-90). An attacker supplying `BenchmarkTest00021=*` (or `*)(` sequences) alters the search filter logic before it reaches the directory.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted HTTP input is concatenated directly into an LDAP search filter string instead of being passed through the JNDI {0} parameterization mechanism (which is correctly used only for the constant street value). No LDAP-specific encoding/escaping (e.g., RFC 4515 filter escaping or ESAPI encodeForLDAP) is applied to `param` before it reaches ctx.search.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: LDAP filter injection: an attacker can inject metacharacters (e.g., `*`, `)`, `(`) to change the search filter logic, enumerate and extract directory records (e.g., all users via a wildcard in the uid clause) whose attributes are echoed back in the HTTP response, or bypass intended query restrictions. Since this sink is a search (read) context, impact is primarily information disclosure rather than object modification.
remediation: Pass the attacker-controlled value as a parameterized argument instead of concatenating it: use filter "(&(objectclass=person)(|(uid={0})))" with filters = new Object[]{param}, so the JNDI LDAP provider treats it as a literal.

If dynamic filter construction is unavoidable, apply LDAP filter escaping of special characters (RFC 4515: \00, (, ), *, \) using a vetted encoder such as ESAPI Encoder.encodeForLDAP before insertion.
Restrict and validate the input against an allowlist (e.g., username character set) as defense in depth.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: HTTP request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00028' read via request.getParameterMap() at lines ~45-49 (param = values[0]). Taint path: param -> line 56 'fileName = org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.Utils.TESTFILES_DIR + param' (direct string concatenation of raw user input onto a fixed directory prefix) -> flagged sink at line 57 'fos = new java.io.FileOutputStream(fileName, false)'. Sanitizers on path: none for this sink. The only encoding call, ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(fileName), executes AFTER the FileOutputStream is constructed and only HTML-encodes the filename echoed back in the response (an anti-XSS measure); it never alters the path string passed to the FileOutputStream. There is no canonicalization, no FilenameUtils.getName(), and no check that the resolved path remains under TESTFILES_DIR, so a param like '../../evil.jsp' or '/etc/cron.d/x' traverses out of the testfiles directory and is passed verbatim to the file-creation sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Raw, unvalidated request-parameter data is concatenated into a filesystem path that is used to create/truncate a file. The parameter can contain '../' sequences or absolute-path components, allowing the JVM process to write outside the intended TESTFILES_DIR. The HTML encoder present in the method is a post-sink, response-output encoder and does not neutralize path traversal.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Arbitrary file creation/overwrite on the server filesystem with the privileges of the application server: attacker can truncate existing files, plant or overwrite configuration, drop content into web-served directories (e.g., a JSP webshell), or write to OS locations such as cron/startup paths, depending on process permissions, potentially leading to remote code execution or denial of service.
remediation: Reject or strip path-manipulation input: canonicalize the candidate path and verify it resolves inside the intended base directory (e.g., File.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(canonicalBase) before opening).
Use a helper such as org.apache.commons.io.FilenameUtils.getName(param) to take only the file name component, and build paths with the base directory + validated name.
Store user-referenced files using server-generated identifiers (e.g., UUID keys in a datastore) rather than raw user-supplied paths.
Harden deployment: run the application with least-privilege filesystem permissions so even a traversal defect cannot write outside designated directories.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: HTTP request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00030' read via request.getParameterMap() and map.get("BenchmarkTest00030")[0] (lines 44-47). The value flows unchanged into local variable 'param' and is passed as the FORMAT STRING argument to response.getWriter().printf(param, obj) at line 53 — the flagged sink. PrintWriter.printf writes every non-format-specifier character of 'param' verbatim into the response body; the response is explicitly declared 'text/html;charset=UTF-8' (line 41), so attacker-supplied markup such as <script>...</script> is reflected into an HTML document with no HTML-encoding, escaping, validator, or output encoder anywhere on the path. The only header manipulation, response.setHeader("X-XSS-Protection", "0") (line 50), does not sanitize — it actively disables the legacy browser XSS filter, worsening the issue. printf's format-specifier handling only affects how the constant objects {"a","b"} are rendered; it does not neutralize the literal attacker text, so it is not an adequate sanitizer for this HTML sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Reflected XSS (CWE-79): untrusted request parameter is written directly into an HTML response body via PrintWriter.printf without any HTML entity encoding or context-aware output escaping; additionally the format string itself is attacker-controlled and the X-XSS-Protection header is explicitly disabled.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: An attacker can craft a URL containing script/HTML in the 'BenchmarkTest00030' parameter; when a victim opens it, arbitrary JavaScript executes in the context of the application origin, enabling session-cookie theft, credential capture, CSRF-style actions as the victim, and content spoofing.
remediation: Do not pass untrusted data as a printf format string or write it raw to the response; pass it as a data argument: response.getWriter().print(Encoder.encodeForHTML(param))
Apply context-aware output encoding (e.g., OWASP Java Encoder's Encode.forHtml) to all reflected input before writing to an HTML response
Remove the response.setHeader("X-XSS-Protection", "0") call and set a Content-Security-Policy to reduce script-execution impact
Validate/allow-list expected input for the parameter at ingestion as defense in depth

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: attacker-controlled HTTP parameter read at lines 45-47 via request.getParameterMap().get("BenchmarkTest00031")[0], assigned to `param`. Sink: line 52 `request.getSession().putValue("userid", param)` stores the raw value directly in the session with no transformation or validation on the path. The only sanitization visible, Utils.encodeForHTML (ESAPI encodeForHTML), is applied exclusively to the response echo at lines 55-58 and is an HTML output encoder — it never touches the value written to the session, and an HTML encoder would not be an adequate mitigation for a session/trust-boundary sink anyway (which requires input validation/allow-listing). Thus untrusted request data crosses into session (trusted) storage unvalidated, satisfying CWE-501.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The servlet copies an HTTP request parameter verbatim into the HTTP session under the security-relevant key 'userid' without validating or constraining it. The encodeForHTML call only sanitizes the reflected output, not the session write, so attacker-controlled data becomes indistinguishable from trusted session state. Whether this escalates to a serious flaw depends on downstream code trusting session.getAttribute("userid") (e.g., for identity/authorization), which is not shown but is the classic exploitation pattern for this sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Trust boundary violation: an attacker can plant arbitrary values into server-side session state under the 'userid' key. If any other component later reads this attribute as trusted (authentication, authorization, audit logging), the attacker could impersonate other users or poison security decisions. Standalone, the impact is limited to unvalidated session-attribute pollution.
remediation: Validate and allow-list the parameter (e.g., strict format/type/range check) before storing it in the session; reject or canonicalize unexpected values.
Do not derive identity or authorization state from client-supplied session attributes; set 'userid' only from the authenticated server-side identity at login.
Treat values read back from the session as untrusted when they originated from request data, and never use them for security decisions without revalidation.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: request.getParameterMap().get("BenchmarkTest00031")[0] (line ~45-47), attacker-controlled HTTP parameter. Flow: param is stored in the session (request.getSession().putValue) and then concatenated into the response written via response.getWriter().println (lines 54-58). However, the attacker-controlled portion is passed through org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.Utils.encodeForHTML(param) immediately before concatenation. The body of that method (shown under 'Called project methods') shows that for a String input it delegates to ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(value), which is the OWASP-recommended HTML-entity output encoder for the HTML body context. The response content type is text/html;charset=UTF-8, matching the encoder's target context. The only attacker-controlled content reaching the sink is the ESAPI-encoded value; the surrounding string literals are constants. No raw, unencoded attacker input reaches the Writer sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The scanner flagged a direct response.getWriter() call pattern, but the tainted parameter is neutralized by ESAPI encoder().encodeForHTML() — a context-appropriate, robust HTML-entity encoder — before being written. The sink receives only properly encoded output, so the flagged XSS path does not exist.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: None for this flagged sink. Note: the raw value is also stored unencoded in the session ('userid'); if that session attribute is later rendered without output encoding in a different sink, XSS could arise there, but that flow is not part of this finding.
remediation: No change required for this finding — retain the ESAPI encodeForHTML call on all reflected output of this parameter.
Ensure the unencoded 'userid' session value is always HTML-encoded (or otherwise context-escaped) wherever it is later read and rendered.
Keep ESAPI encoder configuration (e.g., allowed character sets) under review to ensure the encoding remains effective.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: HttpServletRequest.getParameterMap() at line 43; param = values[0] from request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00034' (lines 45-48) with no validation or encoding. The value flows directly into SQL construction via string concatenation at line 51: "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + param + "'". The tainted string is then passed to the flagged sink at line 56: statement.execute(sql, java.sql.Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS). The statement comes from DatabaseHelper.getSqlStatement(), whose body merely returns conn.createStatement() — a raw java.sql.Statement, not a PreparedStatement, so there is no parameterization. The only helper touched on the path, DatabaseHelper.printResults(), applies ESAPI encodeForHTML only to query OUTPUT written to the response (XSS protection), which does nothing to neutralize SQL metacharacters in the query INPUT. No sanitizer adequate for the SQL execution sink exists anywhere on this path. A payload like ' OR '1'='1 in the parameter breaks out of the PASSWORD literal and alters the query.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted HTTP request parameter is concatenated directly into a SQL query string and executed via a raw java.sql.Statement instead of a parameterized PreparedStatement.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Remote, unauthenticated SQL injection: an attacker can manipulate query logic (authentication bypass on the USERS lookup), extract or modify database contents, and potentially escalate depending on database privileges.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a java.sql.PreparedStatement using a placeholder for the PASSWORD value and set it via setString().
If raw Statement use is unavoidable, strictly validate/allowlist the parameter format before inclusion (defense in depth only; parameterization is the primary fix).
Keep DatabaseHelper.printResults() HTML encoding, but do not rely on it as SQL-input protection.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: HTTP request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00034' read via request.getParameterMap() (lines 44-48: map.get("BenchmarkTest00034") → values[0] → param). The value flows directly into line 52: String sql = "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + param + "'" with no sanitization, validation, or encoding. The tainted string is then passed to the flagged sink at line 56: statement.execute(sql, java.sql.Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS), where statement is a plain java.sql.Statement created via conn.createStatement() in DatabaseHelper.getSqlStatement() — no parameterization. An attacker can supply e.g. ' OR '1'='1 or a UNION SELECT payload as the parameter to alter the query. The only sanitization visible (ESAPI encodeForHTML in DatabaseHelper.printResults) applies to the HTTP response output, after the SQL has already executed, so it does not protect this sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted request-parameter input is concatenated into a SQL query string and executed with java.sql.Statement.execute() instead of a parameterized PreparedStatement, allowing attackers to break out of the PASSWORD string literal and inject arbitrary SQL.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Full SQL injection against the BenchmarkDB datasource: authentication bypass, unauthorized data disclosure (e.g., UNION-based extraction of USERS table contents), and potentially data modification or destruction depending on driver/database capabilities. Any results are echoed back to the attacker via printResults, aiding exfiltration.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized PreparedStatement: connection.prepareStatement("SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD=?") and set the parameter via setString(1, param).
As defense in depth, validate/normalize the input against an allowlist (e.g., expected username/password charset) and ensure the DB account uses least-privilege permissions.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: request.getParameterMap() value for key 'BenchmarkTest00033' (values[0] assigned to `param`, lines 45-49). The raw value flows directly into string concatenation building the SQL statement: "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + param + "'" (line 53). The tainted string `sql` is then passed as the sole argument to org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.DatabaseHelper.JDBCtemplate.queryForRowSet(sql) (lines 55-56), which executes it as a SQL statement. No sanitizer or parameterization exists on this path: the ESAPI encoder().encodeForHTML() calls (lines 61-63 and 69-70) are applied only to query OUTPUT and to the SQL string in error messages, never to `param` before it reaches the SQL sink — HTML encoding would not neutralize SQL metacharacters for this sink anyway. An attacker supplying e.g. BenchmarkTest00033=x' OR '1'='1 breaks out of the quoted literal and arbitrary SQL is executed via JdbcTemplate.queryForRowSet.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Unsanitized HTTP request parameter is concatenated directly into a dynamically constructed SQL statement that is executed via Spring JdbcTemplate.queryForRowSet; no PreparedStatement/parameter binding or SQL-specific input validation is used.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Remote unauthenticated SQL injection: an attacker can manipulate query logic, extract or modify database contents (USERS table includes credential data), and depending on DBMS privileges execute stacked queries or read files, potentially leading to full application/database compromise.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized PreparedStatement: use jdbcTemplate.queryForRowSet("SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD=?", param) or Spring's named-parameter support.
Remove the dangerous dynamic SQL construction pattern and add an allowlist/validation for the parameter if it must influence query structure.
Add regression tests/SAST gating to prevent concatenation of request data into SQL sinks.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: request.getParameterMap() with key 'BenchmarkTest00032' — values[0] is fully attacker-controlled (lines 43-46). Flow: param is concatenated directly into the query string at 'String sql = "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME=\'foo\' and PASSWORD=\'\" + param + \"\'"' (line 53), then passed as the sole argument to DatabaseHelper.JDBCtemplate.execute(sql) at line 54 — the flagged sink. The only encoder on the path, org.owasp.esapi.ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(sql) (line ~56), is applied AFTER execution and only to the string echoed into the HTTP response; it is an HTML output encoder, not a SQL neutralizer, and does not touch the value before it reaches the JDBC sink. No parameterized statement (no '?'/PreparedStatement) and no input validation exists anywhere between source and sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Unsanitized HTTP request parameter is string-concatenated into a SQL statement and executed via JdbcTemplate.execute(), allowing an attacker to break out of the PASSWORD single-quote context and inject arbitrary SQL. No parameterized query or SQL-specific sanitization is applied.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Remote, unauthenticated SQL injection: attacker can alter query logic (authentication bypass against the USERS check), extract or modify database data via boolean/error-based techniques, and, depending on driver/database configuration, execute stacked or destructive statements.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized statement: use JdbcTemplate with a PreparedStatement-style query, e.g. jdbc.execute(con -> { PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD=?"); ps.setString(1, param); ... }) or query(...) with bind parameters.
As defense in depth, validate/normalize the password input against an expected character set before use, and ensure database credentials run with least privileges.
Keep the existing ESAPI encodeForHTML on response output — it is correct for the reflected-output sink but must not be relied upon for the SQL sink.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: request parameters are read via request.getParameterNames() and request.getParameterValues(name). The loop sets param = name for any parameter whose VALUE equals the constant 'BenchmarkTest00036'. Since attackers control both parameter names and values, sending e.g. ?%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C/script%3E=BenchmarkTest00036 makes param the attacker-supplied string '<script>alert(1)</script>'. Flow then goes directly to the flagged sink at line 65: response.getWriter().write(param.toCharArray(), 0, length) with length = param.length(), writing the entire raw string into the response body. The response Content-Type is 'text/html;charset=UTF-8', so the browser renders the bytes as HTML. There is no HTML encoding, output escaping, validator, or sanitizer anywhere on the path; additionally response.setHeader("X-XSS-Protection", "0") explicitly disables the browser's built-in XSS filter, removing a passive mitigation. Source-to-sink path is fully visible in the shown method body and contains zero neutralization, confirming reflected XSS via the parameter name.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Reflected cross-site scripting: an attacker can craft a URL causing arbitrary JavaScript/HTML to execute in the victim's browser in the context of the application's origin, enabling session cookie theft, credential harvesting, defacement, and malicious actions performed as the victim.
remediation: HTML-encode the value before writing it to the response, e.g. encode with OWASP Java Encoder: Encode.forHtml(param) prior to writing
Avoid writing untrusted request data directly to the response Writer/OutputStream; route output through a template/view layer that auto-escapes
Do not disable browser XSS protections; remove the X-XSS-Protection: 0 header and set Content-Security-Policy as defense-in-depth
Whitelist expected parameter names/values instead of echoing attacker-controlled parameter names back into the response
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The servlet echoes attacker-controlled request parameter data (the parameter name) directly into the HTTP response body via response.getWriter().write() with Content-Type text/html and without any output encoding, and even disables the browser XSS auditor, making this a deliberately unmitigated reflected XSS sink (consistent with the OWASP Benchmark vulnerable test case).

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: request.getParameterNames()/getParameterValues() in the doPost loop (lines 45-56). The attacker controls both parameter names and values; when a parameter value equals the constant "BenchmarkTest00037", the variable param is assigned the attacker-supplied parameter NAME (e.g. a request like /?x'%20OR%20'1'='1=BenchmarkTest00037 makes param = "x' OR '1'='1"). Flow: param is concatenated directly into the SQL text at line 65: "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME=? and PASSWORD='" + param + "'". Sink: connection.prepareStatement(sql, ...) at lines 66-71, executed via statement.execute() at line 73. The only binding, statement.setString(1, "foo"), fills the USERNAME placeholder with a constant; the PASSWORD clause containing param remains part of the raw SQL text. No sanitizer, validator, or encoder is applied to param anywhere on the path, and prepareStatement() performs no escaping of embedded quotes in the statement string itself. Attacker-controlled SQL syntax therefore reaches execution.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: User-controlled input (an HTTP parameter name) is concatenated into the SQL statement string instead of being bound as a prepared-statement parameter. The PreparedStatement protects only the '?' placeholder (bound to the constant "foo"), not the string-concatenated PASSWORD clause.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: An attacker can alter the SQL query logic (e.g. break out of the PASSWORD='...' literal with a single quote and append OR conditions, UNION SELECT, or stacked/statement-specific payloads depending on the driver), enabling authentication bypass against this query, unauthorized data extraction from the USERS table, and potentially broader database compromise depending on DB privileges.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a fully parameterized statement: "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME=? and PASSWORD=?" and bind the value via statement.setString(2, param).
As defense in depth, validate/allowlist the parameter name (e.g. pattern ^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$) before using it, since parameter names are attacker-controlled input.
Ensure the database account used by the application has least-privilege permissions to limit the blast radius of any injection.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: request.getParameter("BenchmarkTest00025") (line 44), attacker-controlled. Flow: param is concatenated into sql (line 47: "SELECT userid from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + param + "'"); sql is then passed to org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.DatabaseHelper.JDBCtemplate.queryForObject(sql, Long.class) (lines 51-53). Flagged sink (line 54): response.getWriter().println("Your results are: " + String.valueOf(results)). The value written here is String.valueOf(results), where results is a Long — Spring's queryForObject with requiredType Long coerces the query result to a numeric value (non-numeric results throw DataAccessException instead of returning), so the attacker's raw string never reaches this writer; only digits can be emitted. The one branch that echoes attacker-influenced text ('No results returned for query: ' + sql in the EmptyResultDataAccessException catch) is protected by org.owasp.esapi.ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(sql), which is an adequate HTML output encoder for this text/html response sink. The remaining branch writes only the constant 'Error processing request.'. No unsanitized attacker-controlled string reaches the flagged sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Scanner over-report: the tainted request parameter reaches only the database query string (a CWE-89 SQL-injection sink), while the flagged direct-Writer sink outputs a Long query result derived through queryForObject(sql, Long.class), not the attacker string; the branch that does echo the tainted sql string is HTML-encoded with ESAPI encodeForHTML before writing.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: None for XSS as flagged — attacker input cannot be rendered as script/HTML at line 54. Note the code separately contains SQL injection via string concatenation of param into sql (CWE-89), but that is a different vulnerability class than this finding.
remediation: Replace the string-concatenated sql with a parameterized PreparedStatement/JdbcTemplate query with bound arguments to eliminate the underlying CWE-89 SQL injection.
If any attacker-derived value must be written directly to the Writer, HTML-encode it (e.g., ESAPI encodeForHTML) at every output branch, not just the exception path.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: HttpServletRequest parameters — request.getParameterNames()/request.getParameterValues(name) (lines 46-47). Attacker fully controls both parameter names and values, so an attacker can send a request with parameter name = SQL payload (e.g., ?%' OR '1'='1=BenchmarkTest00038) whose value satisfies the sentinel check value.equals("BenchmarkTest00038"), causing `param = name` (line 53) to be assigned the attacker-chosen parameter name. Flow: param -> string concatenation into `String sql = "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + param + "'"` (line 57) -> executed via org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.DatabaseHelper.JDBCtemplate.query(sql, rowMapper) (lines 59-60), which runs the raw SQL string as a statement (the value is inlined in the SQL, not bound as a JDBC parameter). Sanitizers: none on the taint path. The only encoder present, org.owasp.esapi.ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(...), is applied to the query RESULTS and to the sql string in the exception handler for HTML output — it is not applied to `param` before SQL construction and would not neutralize SQL metacharacters for this sink anyway. The path is complete, reachable, and unsanitized.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Attacker-controlled HTTP request data (the parameter name) is concatenated directly into a SQL query string that is executed via JdbcTemplate.query() as a raw statement instead of using a parameterized PreparedStatement with bind variables.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Unauthenticated SQL injection against the backend database: an attacker can break out of the PASSWORD string literal to alter query logic, extract or modify data (UNION SELECT, stacked/subqueries depending on driver), or potentially execute database-level attacks, depending on the DBMS and account privileges.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized query: pass sql = "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD=?" and bind `param` as an argument to the JdbcTemplate query.

Apply defense-in-depth: validate/allow-list any request-derived values used in queries, run the DB account with least privilege, and disable verbose SQL error exposure (DatabaseHelper.hideSQLErrors should remain enabled).

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: attacker-controlled HTTP request data — request.getParameterNames()/request.getParameterValues(name) (lines 46-56). The loop assigns param = name whenever a parameter's VALUE equals the constant 'BenchmarkTest00039', so an attacker who sends a request with any parameter whose value is 'BenchmarkTest00039' fully controls param via the URL-encoded parameter NAME (e.g. ?%27%20OR%201%3D1--=BenchmarkTest00039 sets param to "' OR 1=1--"). Flow: param -> concatenated directly into the SQL string "SELECT TOP 1 userid from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + param + "'" (lines 64-65) -> passed to DatabaseHelper.JDBCtemplate.queryForMap(sql) (line 67), a raw JDBC execution sink with no parameterization. Sanitizers on path: none for SQL — the only encoder present is ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(), applied to the query RESULTS and to sql only in the exception-message output (lines 70-77); it is an HTML output encoder for XSS that runs after the query executes and does nothing to neutralize SQL metacharacters at the execution sink. The sink is unconditionally reachable inside the try block. This is a complete, unsanitized source-to-sink path.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Attacker-controlled request data (a parameter name harvested from getParameterNames) is concatenated directly into a SQL statement string that is executed via JdbcTemplate.queryForMap without a PreparedStatement/parameterized query or any SQL-specific input validation. The HTML encoding applied to output is not a SQL sanitizer.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Full SQL injection against the backend database: an attacker can alter query logic (e.g. close the PASSWORD quote and append OR conditions or a UNION SELECT to exfiltrate arbitrary table data), perform error-based or blind (boolean/time-based) extraction to dump the USERS table and other database contents, and potentially modify or destroy data depending on database privileges. Only a single-row result is tolerated by queryForMap, but UNION/error/timing payloads trivially accommodate that constraint.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized query: use DatabaseHelper.JDBCtemplate.queryForMap with a PreparedStatement-style SQL string ('... PASSWORD=?') and pass param as a bound argument.
Do not echo user-controlled data into query construction; validate/whitelist the harvested parameter name (e.g. restrict to ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$) if it must be used at all.
Apply least-privilege DB credentials for the application so injected queries cannot escalate to admin-level operations, and keep SQL errors hidden from responses.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: HTTP request parameter 'BenchmarkTest00043' via scr.getTheParameter() (which returns request.getParameter(p) per the shown helper body). Flow: param -> line 49 concatenation 'INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES (\'foo\',\'' + param + '\')' -> line 54 sink statement.executeUpdate(sql, new int[] {1,2}). DatabaseHelper.getSqlStatement() returns a plain java.sql.Statement from conn.createStatement(), so the payload is executed as raw SQL. No sanitizer, validator, or parameterization exists on the path (the null-check defaulting to "" is not sanitization). The ESAPI encodeForHTML in DatabaseHelper.outputUpdateComplete only encodes the query string for HTML display after execution and does not affect the SQL sink.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted request parameter is concatenated directly into an INSERT statement and executed via a dynamic java.sql.Statement instead of a PreparedStatement with bound parameters, allowing an attacker to break out of the single-quoted string literal and inject arbitrary SQL.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL (e.g., param = x');-- or stacked/statement-modifying payloads depending on driver capabilities), leading to unauthorized data modification or disclosure in the BenchmarkDB, and potentially database compromise.
remediation: Replace the concatenated string and java.sql.Statement with a java.sql.PreparedStatement, e.g. conn.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('foo',?)") and bind param via setString(1, param).
Additionally validate/normalize the parameter server-side (allowlist expected format) as defense in depth, and keep DatabaseHelper.hideSQLErrors true to avoid leaking SQL errors to responses.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: request.getParameterValues("BenchmarkTest00044") at line 45; values[0] is assigned to `param` with no validation. The tainted value flows directly into filter construction at line 57: `String filter = "(&(objectclass=person)(uid=" + param + "))";` and reaches the flagged sink at line 61: `ctx.search(base, filter, sc)`, where ctx is a DirContext from LDAPManager.getDirContext() (creates InitialDirContext bound as uid=admin,ou=system per createEnv()). No LDAP-filter escaping or input validation is applied to `param` anywhere on the path. The ESAPI encoder calls in the code are `encodeForHTML` applied only to query RESULTS written to the response and to the filter echoed in the 'nothing found' message — they run after the search and are HTML output encoders, not LDAP filter sanitizers, so they do not neutralize this sink. An attacker can inject filter metacharacters (e.g. param = `*)(uid=*))(|(uid=*`) to alter the search filter's logic, confirming an unsanitized source-to-sink path.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Attacker-controlled HTTP parameter is concatenated directly into an LDAP search filter string without escaping LDAP filter special characters (*, (, ), \, NUL) or validating the input format, allowing the filter's boolean structure to be rewritten.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: LDAP injection: an attacker can manipulate the search filter to bypass intended record restrictions (e.g. enumerate or match arbitrary uid entries under ou=users,ou=system), extract sensitive directory attributes (results are rendered back in the response, enabling data exfiltration), and, because the search runs with an admin-level bind (uid=admin,ou=system), the directory is fully exposed to injected queries rather than constrained by a least-privilege account.
remediation: Encode the untrusted value for LDAP filters before interpolation, e.g. escape all filter metacharacters using an LDAP-filter encoder (OWASP ESAPI Encoder.ldapFilterEncode or equivalent escaping of \, *, (, ), and NUL as \XX).
Alternatively validate `param` against a strict allowlist (e.g. ^[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+$) and reject any value containing LDAP metacharacters.
Bind the directory context with a least-privilege service account instead of uid=admin,ou=system so injected queries cannot reach privileged objects.
Return a generic response for both found/not-found cases to avoid using the endpoint as an oracle for blind LDAP enumeration.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: attacker-controlled HTTP query string via request.getQueryString() (line 43). The value of the 'BenchmarkTest00048' parameter is extracted with queryString.indexOf(paramval) and queryString.substring(paramLoc + paramval.length(), ...) (lines 46-61), so fully attacker-controlled bytes reach 'param'. The only transformation on the path is java.net.URLDecoder.decode(param, "UTF-8") (line 68), which merely percent-decodes the value and is NOT a sanitizer for HTML output - it can actually reintroduce <, >, " characters from %-encoding. The flagged sink at line 72, response.getWriter().print(param.toCharArray()), writes the raw value into the response body while the content type is 'text/html;charset=UTF-8' (line 41), so browsers render it as HTML. No HTML encoding, output escaping, or allow-list validation exists anywhere on the path, and response.setHeader("X-XSS-Protection", "0") (line 71) explicitly disables the legacy browser XSS filter. A request like GET ?BenchmarkTest00048=%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C/script%3E executes attacker JavaScript in the victim's browser.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Reflected XSS: attacker-controlled query-string data is written directly to the HTML response body via response.getWriter().print() without any HTML-aware output encoding; URLDecoder.decode only handles percent-encoding and provides no neutralization of HTML metacharacters, and the XSS auditor header is explicitly disabled.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Reflected cross-site scripting: an attacker can craft a URL that executes arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the application's origin when a victim clicks it, enabling session-cookie theft, credential harvesting, defacement, and actions performed as the victim.
remediation: HTML-encode the value before writing it to the response, e.g. encode with OWASP Java Encoder: response.getWriter().print(Encode.forHtml(param));
Alternatively, set the response Content-Type to a non-HTML type such as text/plain when the data is not intended to be rendered as markup.
Remove response.setHeader("X-XSS-Protection", "0") and do not rely on browser-side filtering; apply server-side output encoding contextual to the sink.
Validate/allow-list the expected parameter value format before echoing it back to the client.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: HTTP parameter `request.getParameterValues("BenchmarkTest00045")` at line 44, taken verbatim into `param = values[0]` (no validation). The value flows into `String fileName = org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.Utils.TESTFILES_DIR + param;` (line 48) via direct string concatenation, then reaches the sink `new java.io.FileOutputStream(new java.io.FileInputStream(fileName).getFD())` (lines 61-62), where the attacker-controlled path is used to open a file for reading and obtain a FileOutputStream on the same descriptor. No sanitizer, validator, canonicalization, or filename extraction (e.g., FilenameUtils.getName) is applied to `param` or `fileName` before the sink; a '../' payload in the parameter traverses out of TESTFILES_DIR. The only encoding present, `ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(fileName)`, is applied solely to the response output (XSS encoding) and has no effect on the file path. The try-with-resources sink and catch block confirm the path is used directly for filesystem access.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Unsanitized, attacker-controlled request parameter is concatenated directly into a filesystem path that is opened for read/write (FileInputStream -> getFD -> FileOutputStream), permitting path traversal sequences like '../' to escape the intended TESTFILES_DIR directory.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: An attacker can point the path at arbitrary locations on the server filesystem: opening/reading arbitrary readable files (error messages can leak existence/behavior) and, because a FileOutputStream is created on the same file descriptor, potentially overwriting file contents from the current position — enabling arbitrary file access and possible tampering with the application's privileges.
remediation: Reject or strip path traversal sequences and path separators from the user input before using it in a file path
Resolve the canonical path (File.getCanonicalPath()) and verify it still starts with the intended TESTFILES_DIR before opening
Prefer extracting only the filename component (e.g., org.apache.commons.io.FilenameUtils.getName(param)) and allowlisting expected filenames instead of accepting full paths
Avoid chaining FileInputStream.getFD() into FileOutputStream; open the target file explicitly with validated, application-controlled paths

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Attacker-controlled source: request.getQueryString() (HTTP query string, fully attacker-supplied). Flow: queryString.indexOf("BenchmarkTest00049=") locates the parameter (lines 43-46); param = queryString.substring(paramLoc + paramval.length(), ampersandLoc) (lines 59-68) extracts the raw attacker value; param = java.net.URLDecoder.decode(param, "UTF-8") (line 71) percent-decodes the value — this is NOT a sanitizer and actually reconstitutes characters like < > " from %3C %3E %22. Sink: response.getWriter().write("Parameter value: " + param) at line 72 writes the value directly into an HTTP response body served as text/html;charset=UTF-8 (set at line 41). No HTML encoder, validator, or output-escaping exists anywhere on the path. Additionally, line 72 sets the header X-XSS-Protection: 0, explicitly disabling browser XSS filtering. Example exploit: GET /?BenchmarkTest00049=%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C/script%3E causes the decoded <script>alert(1)</script> to be written into the HTML response and executed in the victim's browser.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Reflected cross-site scripting (CWE-79): an attacker can craft a URL that injects arbitrary JavaScript/HTML into the page rendered in a victim's browser, enabling session-cookie theft, credential phishing, defacement, or drive-by delivery of further attacks against application users.
remediation: HTML-encode the value before writing it to the response, e.g. use the OWASP Java Encoder: response.getWriter().write("Parameter value: " + Encoder.forHtml(param));

If shell invocation is unavoidable, strictly validate the input against an allowlist (e.g. ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]*$) and reject or drop special shell metacharacters (;, |, &, $, `, <, >, \, ", ').
Prefer safe library APIs over shelling out, and add regression tests covering command injection payloads in cookie/header parameters.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: cookie value 'BenchmarkTest00097' read from request.getCookies() and URL-decoded into 'param' (lines ~55-63) — attacker-controlled. org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The ternary condition (7*18)+num > 200 (232 > 200) always evaluates true, so 'bar' is always assigned the constant "This_should_always_happen" and the attacker-controlled cookie value 'param' never propagates to the response writer. The scanner flagged the Writer call without resolving the ternary or the encoder.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: None — no attacker-controlled data reaches the response output, and even if it did it would be HTML-encoded, preventing reflected XSS.
remediation: No fix required; the flagged sink is safe as written.
Optionally simplify the misleading tautological ternary and remove the dead 'param' assignment to reduce scanner noise.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Full SQL injection: an attacker controlling the cookie can break out of the PASSWORD string literal to alter query logic, extract arbitrary data from the USERS table or other database objects (potential authentication bypass / data exfiltration), and depending on database privileges cause data modification or denial of service via injected SQL errors.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized query, e.g. JDBCtemplate.queryForMap("SELECT TOP 1 userid from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='?'", bar) using Spring's PreparedStatement argument binding so the value is never parsed as SQL.

Ensure the database account used by the application has least-privilege permissions to limit impact of any residual injection, and keep DatabaseHelper.hideSQLErrors behavior (generic errors) enabled to avoid leaking query details.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The no-direct-response-writer rule misfired: although tainted header data enters the method, it is only concatenated into a SQL string; the value actually written to the flagged Writer sink at line 63 is a type-coerced Integer query result, the tainted SQL echoed in the EmptyResultDataAccessException handler is neutralized by ESAPI encodeForHTML, and the DataAccessException handler writes a constant. org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: None for XSS as flagged. Note separately (out of scope of this finding): the tainted header is concatenated into a SQL statement at line 55 executed via queryForObject, which is a SQL injection risk that should be assessed under the relevant CWE-89 rule.
