org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: A raw, attacker-controlled query-string value is reflected directly into the HTTP response body via Writer.format with %s substitution and no HTML output encoding, while the browser XSS filter is explicitly disabled.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: Reflected cross-site scripting: attacker-crafted URLs execute arbitrary JavaScript in victims' browsers, enabling session/cookie theft, credential capture, and defacement; the disabled X-XSS-Protection header removes a legacy mitigation layer.
remediation: HTML-encode bar (e.g., OWASP Encoder.encodeForHTML or ESAPI encodeForHTML) before writing it into the response body.
Prefer a templating/view technology with automatic contextual escaping instead of raw Writer output.
Remove the 'X-XSS-Protection: 0' header; apply a Content-Security-Policy as defense in depth.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: HTTP request data in doPost — the loop over request.getParameterNames()/getParameterValues() sets param = name (the attacker-chosen parameter NAME whose value equals the constant 'BenchmarkTest00573'), so param is fully attacker-controlled. Flow: param -> bar (line 57) -> String[] argsEnv = {bar} (line 63) -> Runtime r.exec(cmd, argsEnv) (line ~70, the flagged sink). The FIRST argument of exec (the command itself) is cmd, produced by Utils.getInsecureOSCommandString(), whose body (shown) returns only a fixed absolute path to 'insecureCmd.bat'/'insecureCmd.sh' resolved from the classpath via System.getProperty("os.name") — it is never tainted. Thus the attacker-controlled value lands exclusively in the SECOND exec parameter (envp), i.e., the child process environment block. Environment entries passed via Runtime.exec(String, String[]) are transmitted as data (the execve environ array / CreateProcess environment block) and are never parsed, expanded, or executed as command text at this sink, so no shell metacharacter or argument injection into the command line is possible here. The only other taint use is reflected output, which Utils.printOSCommandResults (shown) encodes with ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML before writing to the response, adequately covering that sink. No path exists from attacker input to the command string or its arguments, so CWE-78 is not demonstrable.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The scanner sees tainted HTTP input reaching a Runtime.exec overload, but mis-attributes the risk: the tainted value is passed as the process-environment array (envp), not as the command or its arguments. The command string is a constant classpath-derived path. Environment variables are passed as opaque data to the child process and are not interpreted as OS command syntax, so the flagged CWE-78 sink is not attacker-controllable. (The rule also misfires on safe APIs here — exec(cmd, envp) with a fixed cmd.)
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: None as OS command injection. Worst theoretical effect is manipulation of the environment of the fixed insecureCmd script (its body is not shown, and the entire environment is replaced by the single attacker-supplied entry); this would require the script itself to act unsafely on environment values, which is not demonstrated and is outside the flagged CWE-78 sink.
remediation: Do not pass attacker-controlled data into Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder environment arrays; validate against a strict whitelist (e.g., ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]*$) or use a constant instead.
Keep the executed command fully static (as it is today) and ensure any future change never interpolates request data into the command string or arguments.

If environment data must reach the child process, pass it through a well-defined channel (e.g., stdin, with encoding handled by the child) rather than arbitrary env entries, and document the expected format in insecureCmd.sh/.bat.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: line 43 `request.getParameter("BenchmarkTest01290")` is attacker-controlled. Flow: `param` (line 43) → `new Test().doSomething(request, param)` at line 46 (body of Test.doSomething not provided, but even assuming full pass-through) → `String[] argsEnv = {bar}` (line 52) → sink `r.exec(cmd, argsEnv)` (line 56). The command string `cmd` comes from `Utils.getInsecureOSCommandString(...)`, whose shown body returns a constant absolute path to `insecureCmd.bat`/`insecureCmd.sh` loaded from the classpath — no taint reaches the command or its argument vector. Additionally, `Runtime.exec` does not invoke a shell, so environment values are never parsed/interpreted as commands, and there is no code path by which the attacker value can alter which program is executed or with what arguments. Output of the process is HTML-encoded via ESAPI in `Utils.printOSCommandResults`, so no secondary XSS either. The rule misfired by treating any tainted value appearing inside the exec() call as reaching the command position.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The scanner flags any tainted data inside a Runtime.exec() call, but the actual overload used here (`exec(String command, String[] envp)`) places the tainted value in the process environment block. The executed command is a constant classpath-derived path, so the attacker cannot control the command string or its arguments, which is what CWE-78 requires. (Note: Test.doSomething's body was not shown, but this gap is irrelevant to the decision since even full taint propagation only reaches the envp parameter.)
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: None in the shown code path — the attacker value is at most an environment variable (and entries without '=' are typically discarded). Had the taint reached the command string or argument vector, the impact would be arbitrary OS command execution with the server's privileges.
remediation: Keep the command string and any process arguments strictly constant/whitelisted; never interpolate request data into the command or argument positions of Runtime.exec/ProcessBuilder.
If HTTP-derived values must be passed to a child process, map them through a strict allowlist of known names and values, and validate format (e.g., ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$) before placing them in envp.
Prefer an allowlist lookup (e.g., permitted command IDs mapped to fixed commands) instead of forwarding raw user input anywhere into process-execution APIs.

Flow: param -> new Test().doSomething(request, param) (line 59) -> bar -> concatenated into String filter = "(&(objectclass=person))(|(uid=" + bar + ")(street={0}))" -> flagged sink ctx.search(base, filter, filters, sc) at line 73, executed against a real DirContext (LDAPManager.getDirContext binds as uid=admin to ldap://localhost:10389 per the shown helper bodies). The decisive unknown is Test.doSomething(): its body is NOT present under 'Called project methods' (only LDAPManager methods are provided), so whether 'bar' is LDAP-neutralized inside that transformation cannot be verified from the code shown. Source-to-sink reachability is demonstrated, but the sanitization decision depends on the missing doSomething body, so exploitability cannot be proven or disproven from the visible code.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The LDAP search filter is built by string concatenation from request-derived data. Within the visible method no LDAP-specific encoding/escaping (e.g., ESAPI encodeForLDAP/encodeForLDAPFilter or a metacharacter whitelist) is applied before ctx.search(); the only encoders are HTML encoders applied post-query. However, the required transformation happens inside Test.doSomething(request, param), whose body was not supplied, so the presence or absence of a sanitizer adequate for this sink cannot be confirmed. If doSomething leaves param effectively intact, this is a classic CWE-90 LDAP injection; if it neutralizes metacharacters, it is safe.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: If the taint passes through doSomething unneutralized: an attacker can manipulate the LDAP search filter to alter query semantics, enumerate or read directory entries they should not see, and potentially influence application behavior keyed on the search result; the context binds with admin credentials, so query manipulation runs with full directory read privileges. Note the static filter string is already structurally unusual ('(&(objectclass=person))(|(uid=...)(street={0}))'), which may itself limit how far a server accepts injected clauses.
remediation: Inspect/fix Test.doSomething and ensure no attacker-controlled data is concatenated into LDAP filter strings; use the JNDI parameterized form ctx.search(base, "(&(objectclass=person)(|(uid={0})(street={1})))", args, sc) instead of building filter strings by concatenation.
If dynamic filter text is unavoidable, apply an LDAP-filter-specific escaper such as OWASP ESAPI Encoder.encodeForLDAPFilter()/encodeForLDAP() on the untrusted value before interpolation.

Validate input against a strict allowlist (e.g., alphanumeric uid pattern) before it is used in any directory query, and bind the application's LDAP connection with a least-privilege account rather than admin credentials.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: attacker-controlled HTTP input via request.getQueryString() (line 41). The value is parsed out with indexOf/substring (lines 43-62) and passed through java.net.URLDecoder.decode (line 63), which only URL-decodes and does not neutralize SQL metacharacters. It then flows into 'new Test().doSomething(request, param)' (line 64); the OWASP Benchmark shared helper (org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.Test) only performs a Base64 encode-then-decode round-trip, a taint-preserving identity transformation with no SQL sanitization, and returns it as 'bar'. 'bar' is concatenated at line 66 into sql = "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + bar + "'". Sink: org.owasp.benchmark.helpers.DatabaseHelper.JDBCtemplate.query(sql, RowMapper) at lines 67-68 — the raw-SQL String overload of Spring JdbcTemplate with no ? placeholders and no bound parameters, so the tainted value is executed as part of the SQL statement. The ESAPI encodeForHTML calls (lines 91, 97) are output encoders applied only to query results/error text AFTER execution and do not protect this sink. No sanitizer, validator, or parameterization adequate for the SQL sink exists anywhere on the source-to-sink path.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: Untrusted query-string data is concatenated directly into a SQL statement and executed via the non-parameterized JdbcTemplate.query(String, RowMapper) overload, with no SQL-specific sanitization or parameter binding on the path.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: SQL injection against the USERS table: an attacker can break out of the PASSWORD literal and alter the query (e.g., OR '1'='1', UNION SELECT, stacked/subquery payloads) to read or manipulate arbitrary database data available to the application's DB account, including authentication bypass and data exfiltration via UNION or error-based techniques.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized query: use sql = "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD=?" and call JDBCtemplate.query(sql, rowMapper, bar) so the value is bound, never parsed as SQL.
As defense in depth, validate/normalize the expected input format server-side and apply least-privilege DB credentials so injected queries cannot reach sensitive objects.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: request.getQueryString() (line ~43) is fully attacker-controlled. The parameter value is carved out via queryString.indexOf("BenchmarkTest01731="), substring extraction, and java.net.URLDecoder.decode(param, "UTF-8") (lines 43-63) — none of which is SQL sanitization (URL-decoding only decodes percent-escapes; it leaves single quotes intact and even introduces new metacharacters from encoded input). The value then flows into `new Test().doSomething(request, param)` (line 65) whose return value `bar` is concatenated at line 71 into `String sql = "SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME='foo' and PASSWORD='" + bar + "'"` and executed via the flagged sink `statement.execute(sql, ...)` (line 77) using a plain java.sql.Statement from DatabaseHelper.getSqlStatement() (shown: conn.createStatement(), no prepared statement). The shown helper methods (printResults, getSqlConnection) contain no SQL sanitization and are not on the taint path into the query. The ONLY possible neutralization point on this path is the body of Test.doSomething, which is NOT provided in 'Called project methods'. The visible code therefore traces a complete source-to-sink path except for the single deciding transformation, which is genuinely not visible from the shown code.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The servlet builds a SQL string by string concatenation and executes it with java.sql.Statement.execute, a pattern that is vulnerable to SQL injection if `bar` retains attacker influence. URLDecoder.decode is not a SQL sanitizer, and no parameterized query, escaping, or encoding adequate for this sink appears anywhere in the visible path. However, the taint passes through Test.doSomething(request, param), whose body was not provided; in this codebase that method sometimes returns the tainted param largely intact (vulnerable variant) and sometimes discards it for a constant or encodes it (safe variant). Whether CWE-89 holds depends entirely on that unseen body, so the final sanitization decision is not answerable from the code shown.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: If Test.doSomething passes tainted data through (or only cosmetically transforms it), an attacker can close the PASSWORD literal with a single quote and inject arbitrary SQL against the BenchmarkDB connection (e.g., ' OR '1'='1' -- to bypass authentication logic in the query, or stacked/malformed queries depending on driver capabilities), potentially reading or modifying data accessible to the application's database account. Note the raw or error-driven feedback path: DatabaseHelper.hideSQLErrors controls whether SQLException details are thrown back as a ServletException, which can enable error-based exploitation.
remediation: Replace string concatenation with a parameterized query: use conn.prepareStatement("SELECT * from USERS where USERNAME=? and PASSWORD=?") and bind values via setString(), never interpolating request data into SQL text.
Inspect and fix Test.doSomething: it must not return attacker-controlled data for use in SQL; if a transformation is needed for other sinks, keep the SQL path on the original typed parameters.
If dynamic SQL is unavoidable, apply a SQL-specific encoder (e.g., ESAPI encodeForSQL with the correct codec/dialect) on every tainted component — URL/HTML encoding is not adequate for this sink.
Set DatabaseHelper.hideSQLErrors appropriately and avoid surfacing SQLException details to clients; grant the application's DB account least-privilege to limit SQL injection blast radius.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Flagged sink: `idc.search(base, filter, sc)` at line 62, where `filter = "(&(objectclass=person)(uid=" + bar + "))"` (line ~54). That constant flows into `new Test().doSomething(request, param)` (body not provided) to produce `bar`, then into the filter string and the `search()` call. No LDAP-specific neutralization (encodeForLDAP / RFC 4515 filter escaping) exists anywhere on the path; the ESAPI `encodeForHTML` calls apply only to query results and the 'nothing found' message AFTER the search executes (output encoding for XSS), and are irrelevant to the LDAP sink. org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The rule misfired: the source method's shown body returns the literal constant "bar" instead of request data, so no attacker-controlled value is demonstrably concatenated into the LDAP filter. This would only be a true positive if `Test.doSomething(request, param)` ignored its constant argument and independently derived `bar` from the raw request object — its body is not shown, which is the sole reason confidence is not high. Also note there is genuinely no LDAP-filter escaping on the path; the code is safe only because the input is constant, not because it is sanitized.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: If the flow were attacker-controlled, `bar` interpolated into `(uid=BAR)` without escaping would allow LDAP filter injection (e.g., `*)(objectClass=*` to alter filter logic), enabling directory enumeration, unauthorized record disclosure, or authentication-logic bypass against the LDAP tree; the search runs with admin credentials (uid=admin).
remediation: If request-derived values are ever passed to this flow, escape all LDAP filter metacharacters before interpolation (e.g., ESAPI encoder().encodeForLDAP() or RFC 4515 escaping of * ( ) \ NUL), or use parameterized search controls instead of string concatenation.

Enforce strict whitelisted format validation on user-supplied identifiers (e.g., ^[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+$) before they are embedded in any LDAP filter, and avoid granting the application's LDAP bind account admin-level privileges.
